trade: Maths and map class with the levee district's planner — learner and levee district planner
header: Lower-secondary maths at the Lakefront Levee and Floodwall Crew in Jefferson Parish: a flood map as a coloured data display, read through its key, its scale and its north arrow, low ground told apart from high ground, and the map used to plan a route and a meeting place, using only the practice map the scene shows.
name: Reading a Flood Map's Colours
tagline: Key first, then colours — a flood map shows low and high ground so a family can plan calmly

badge.name: Map Key Reader
badge.note: Read a practice flood map through its key and scale, told low ground from high and planned a route to higher ground

hazards.label: Decide what each colour means without reading the key?
hazards.text: You guessed what the colours mean. Different maps use colours differently, so the key is the only honest guide. Read the key first, then the map; a colour means exactly what the key says and nothing else.

hazards.label: Say the map shows where water is right now?
hazards.text: You said the map shows today's water. A flood map shows which ground is lower or more likely to hold water in heavy rain, so people can plan ahead. It is a planning tool, not a live picture of the streets.

hazards.label: Judge the distance to higher ground by eye?
hazards.text: You judged the distance by eye. Maps are drawn smaller than real life, and the scale bar tells you by how much. Measure along the route and use the scale bar, or your plan could be far longer or shorter than you think.

hazards.label: Say a family on higher ground needs no plan at all?
hazards.text: You said families on higher ground need no plan. Every family benefits from a plan: roads you use may cross low ground, and neighbours may need help. The map helps everyone plan, wherever they live.

find1.title: Find the three tools on the map
find1.cue: Mark the three parts of the practice map you read before looking at any colours.
find1.why: Every good map carries three tools. The key tells you what each colour means, the scale bar tells you how map distance turns into real distance, and the north arrow tells you which way the map faces. Reading those first is the difference between looking at a pretty picture and actually reading a map.
items: It says what each colour means.
It turns map distance into real distance.
It shows which way the map faces.
decoy: Nice to look at, but it tells you nothing about the ground.

select1.title: Sit at the planning table
select1.cue: Take your seat at the planner's table before the practice map is unrolled.
select1.why: The planner's table is where the levee district lays out its maps and talks through plans. Sitting there means everyone can see the whole map at once and point to what they mean. Planners work round a shared table for the same reason: a plan made together is understood together.
select1.label: Sit at the table

seq.title: Put the map-reading steps in order
seq.cue: Read the title, read the key, find where you are, then read the colours around you.
seq.why: The title tells you what the map is about, the key tells you how to read it, finding yourself anchors the map to the real world, and only then do the colours around you make sense. Reading in that order stops you jumping to a conclusion before you know what the colours mean.
seq.oon: Out of order. Read the map's title and key before you look at any colours.

hold.title: Keep your finger on the school
hold.cue: Hold your finger on the school's symbol while your partner reads the colour around it.
hold.why: On a busy map it is easy to lose the spot you were reading. Holding your place while a partner reads the colour against the key means you both talk about the same place. Planners pin a marker to the map in the same way, so the conversation stays on the spot that matters.
hold.brk: Your finger slid off the school. Find its symbol again and hold it there.
hold.label: Finger on the school

turn.title: Turn the map to face north
turn.cue: Turn the map dial until the north arrow points the same way as the compass on the table.
turn.why: When a map faces the same way as the real world, left on the map is left outside and routes are easier to follow. Lining the north arrow up with a compass is called setting the map. Crews set their maps before every job in the field so no one heads off the wrong way.
turn.label: Map set to north

gauge.title: Measure the route with the scale bar
gauge.cue: Commit when the measuring strip matches the length of the route on the scale bar.
gauge.why: The scale bar is a ruler for the map. Laying your strip along the route and then against the scale bar turns a map length into a real distance. Knowing the real distance lets a family judge whether a route is a short walk or needs a car, which is the kind of choice a good plan makes early.
gauge.label: Route length
gauge.miss: Not matched yet. Line the strip up against the scale bar carefully.

drag.title: Place the meeting pin on higher ground
drag.cue: Drag the meeting pin to a place the key shows as higher ground.
drag.why: A family meeting place works best somewhere easy to reach and on higher ground. Using the key to choose it, rather than guessing, means the choice is based on the map's evidence. Planners choose staging areas and shelters in the same careful way, colour by colour.
drag.label: Meeting pin
drag.miss: That spot is not higher ground on the key. Check the key and try again.

select2.title: Choose the route that stays on higher ground
select2.cue: Choose the route from school to the meeting pin that crosses the least low ground.
select2.why: Two routes can be the same length but cross very different ground. Reading the colours along each route and choosing the one that stays higher is using the map as intended: to make a calm, sensible plan ahead of time. That is exactly how the planner helps crews choose their roads.
select2.label: Choose the route

find2.title: Spot the mistakes in a sample map reading
find2.cue: Look at another group's notes on the map and mark each mistake.
find2.why: Map readings go wrong in familiar ways: a colour read without the key, a distance guessed instead of measured, or a map that was upside down. Finding these in someone else's notes trains the careful habits that make your own reading trustworthy.
items: a colour read without checking the key
decoy: the map's title written at the top of the notes

track.title: Trace the route along the streets
track.cue: Keep the marker on your chosen route as you trace it along the streets on the map.
track.why: Tracing the route slowly shows every turn and every change of colour along the way. You might notice a stretch that dips into low ground or a bridge you had not seen. Planners trace routes the same way before a crew sets off, so there are no surprises on the road.
track.brk: The marker left the route. Find the street again and keep tracing.
track.label: Route traced

record.title: Record your map reading
record.cue: Write what the key says, your meeting place, your route and its real distance.
record.why: Written notes turn a map reading into a plan anyone can follow. Recording what the key says beside your choices shows your reasons, so a grown-up can check them. The levee district keeps notes like these with every map it uses, so plans can be shared and improved.
record.label: Map reading record

share.title: Check your plan with the planner
share.cue: Show the planner your route and meeting place and ask if they would choose the same.
share.why: The planner knows the parish's roads and the map's details well. Checking your plan with someone who uses these maps every day tests your reading. If they suggest a change, it is usually because of something on the ground the map alone cannot show.
share.label: Check with the planner

checkin.title: Check in at the planning table
checkin.cue: What did the key help you see? How could a map like this help your family plan?
checkin.why: The planner closes each meeting by asking what everyone will do next, so the class closes the same way. Each learner names one thing the key showed and one way a family could use a map to plan calmly. Anyone who found the map worrying can say so, and the group talks about how planning helps.
checkin.label: End-of-session check-in

interrupts.label: Put the weights on the map's corners
interrupts.alert: The practice map starts to roll up and the group's markers slide off.
interrupts.cue: Put the weights on the map's corners so it lies flat again.
interrupts.why: A map that keeps moving is hard to read accurately, and markers end up in the wrong place. Weighting the corners fixes the map so everyone reads the same spot. Planners do this before every meeting for exactly this reason.
interrupts.miss: Nobody weighted the corners, and the markers slid into the wrong places as the map kept rolling up.
interrupts.wrong: That does not hold the map flat. Put the weights on the corners. Choose the response that deals with it now.
interrupts.done: Map weighted flat, markers replaced. The lesson carries on.

interrupts.label: Read the colour from the key
interrupts.alert: The planner points to a colour on the map and asks what it means.
interrupts.cue: Check the key and say what that colour stands for.
interrupts.why: Going to the key, rather than guessing, is the habit the whole lesson teaches. Saying what the key says shows you read the map honestly. The planner asks because a wrong guess can lead to a poor plan.
interrupts.miss: You guessed the colour's meaning without checking the key, and the planner had to show you the key before the group could go on.
interrupts.wrong: That is a guess. Check the key first. Choose the response that deals with it now.
interrupts.done: Colour read from the key. The lesson carries on.

guide.hazard: Stop. Check the key — do not guess.

lateRecord: The map reading is recorded once the route is chosen — nothing to record yet.
lateCheckin: The check-in comes at the very end of the session.
